title: Every day is blessed
hookLine: the days, months and moments are blessed for those on whom grace falls (Barah Maha, ang 136)

cards: Which date to marry on? Which morning to sign the lease? Which hour to start the journey?
Plenty of calendars mark some days as lucky and others as not. In Punjab, the first day of each solar month, when the sun moves into a new sign, is called Sangrand.
On Sangrand many gurdwaras hold a special gathering, and the Barah Maha stanza for the new month is read aloud. So you might expect the poem to end by naming its best month. It doesn't.

teach.h: MONTHS, DAYS, MOMENTS: BLESSED BY GRACE.
teach.b: The closing stanza says, in paraphrase: the months, the days and the moments are blessed for those on whom the Lord casts His glance of grace. Nanak begs for the gift of Your sight; be merciful, Lord.
Moorat, the word for moment, is the same word people use for an auspicious hour, and the stanza simply hands every hour to grace.

teach.h: NO MONTH IS HOLY BY ITSELF.
teach.b: No month in the poem is holy by itself. Chet isn't better than Poh. What makes a day blessed is whether it's lived in the Lord's sight.
Sikhs hold Sangrand in two ways, and this stanza speaks to both. Many keep it gladly: a monthly gathering, a reason to come to the gurdwara, a chance to hear the new month's stanza and begin again.
Some are wary of Sangrand becoming a lucky day, and point to this closing to say no date carries power of its own. Both are trying to honor the same line. Now look back at the whole poem.
It began with a year of longing, and a bride separated by her own deeds. Chet brought joy in remembering. Vaisakh, longing.
Jeth, bowing. Asarh, keeping Him near in the heat. Sawan, blossoming.
Bhadon, doubt. Assu, how to meet. Katak, blaming no one.
Maghar, sitting together. Poh, held warm. Magh, the humble bath.
And the last stanza says every one of them, even the doubt, can be a blessed month. Every month is His.

how: On Sangrand, the first day of each solar month, many gurdwaras hold a special diwan where the new month's stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha is read; some Sikhs keep the day gladly, while others stress that the poem's closing makes every day equally blessed.

the first day of each month in the solar calendar
the luckiest day of the year to start a journey

it says the months, days and moments are blessed for those on whom grace falls.
on Sangrand, many gurdwaras read the new month's stanza
it's a monthly gathering to hear the Barah Maha's line for the month ahead.
all Sikhs view Sangrand in exactly the same way

games.q: you're choosing the date for something important. what does the Barah Maha's closing stanza say makes a day blessed?
o: picking the first day of the month.
games.why: the months, days and moments are blessed for those on whom the Lord casts His glance of grace. no date carries power by itself.

practice: Sit with the breath and let today count, ordinary as it is. Let one month's line from this block come back, Assu, how to meet, or Poh, held warm, whichever you need today, and rest in it for a few breaths.
If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between breaths.

wordCard.voice: Sangrand. The first day of a solar month, when gurdwaras read that month's stanza of the Barah Maha; and the poem's closing says every day is blessed when grace falls on it.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Sangrand, the Punjabi form of Sanskrit sankranti, the sun's passing into a new sign.

carryVoice: Your line: every month is his. Even a hard day is still His day. Day five hundred seventy-eight, and a whole year of months.

sources.ref: Barah Maha, Raag Majh, Mahalla 5, closing stanza (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136)
